lessons.title: فهم (fahima) — "he understood," and the vowel that makes a state
lessons.gloss: "he understood" — the first verb whose middle vowel is not an a, marking it a state rather than a deed, and the done-to shape that turns it into the word for a concept

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Six verbs so far, every one of them a deed. This one is not: it happens inside a person — and Arabic marks that in the vowels.
Nothing new in فهم (fahima) itself: ف (fāʾ, one dot), ه (hāʾ) and م (mīm), with fāʾ's two-dotted partner ق the pair sorted out in ʿarafa. That is twice running — أكل needed no new letters either.

One letter does need naming, because every word-family ahead reaches for it: و (wāw). You have read it unnamed inside قَوْل (qawl), "a saying." It is a non-joiner, a small loop with a tail under the line, and it holds two jobs — the consonant w, and the long vowel ū.
فَهِمَ (fahima) = "he understood." Root ف-ه-م.

Listen to the middle vowel. Dhahaba, qāla, ʿarafa and akala all ran a-a-a, the فَعَلَ (faʿala) shape. Fahima runs a-i-a: فَعِلَ (faʿila), which Arabic keeps for states rather than deeds. Understanding is not performed; it arrives.
فَهْم (fahm) — "understanding," the bare thing.
مَفْهوم (mafhūm) — "understood," the done-to shape of mashkūr and maqūl, its long ū riding that و. As a noun it is "a concept": a thing that has been understood.
And the flat statement akala insisted on holds here too: ف-ه-م has no English relative. Fathom is Germanic; the resemblance is noise. No Hebrew twin worth the claim, either.

lessons.title: قرأ (qaraʾa) — "he recited," and the word English spells Quran
lessons.gloss: "he read, he recited" — hamza's three seats sorted out at last, and the one root in this chapter that really did give English a word

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: One root in this chapter did give English a word — exactly one, and it is not the word for reading.
ق (qāf, two dots) and ر (rāʾ) are yours. The third is أ, hamza on an alif seat, closing the word.
Hamza is the homeless consonant. It has a sound of its own — the catch in "uh-oh" — but usually no letter, so it borrows a seat, and which seat depends on the vowels around it:
أ — hamza on ا, as in قَرَأَ and in أنت.
ؤ — hamza on و, the letter named last lesson.
ئ — hamza on ي, which gives up its dots to carry it.
ء — and where no seat suits, hamza alone on the line, closing جاء.
Four spellings, one consonant. The seat is bookkeeping; the hamza is the sound.
قَرَأَ (qaraʾa) = "he read" — nearer the root's heart, "he recited aloud." Reading here is done with the voice. Root ق-ر-أ, plain faʿala shape.
قارِئ (qāriʾ) — "a reader," the doer shape of qāʾil, hamza on its dotless yāʾ seat.
مَقْروء (maqrūʾ) — "read," the done-to shape of mafhūm, long ū on the و, hamza left seatless at the end.
قُرْآن (qurʾān) — "the recitation," the thing recited. English writes it Quran, or Koran. Its long آ is the alif-and-hamza fusion already met in آكِل (ākil), "an eater."

That single loan is the shape of the whole story. Arabic gave English algebra, alcohol, coffee, sugar and admiral — goods and sciences, nouns nearly every one. Out of ق-ر-أ travelled not "to read" but the name of a book. The nearer relative is Hebrew קָרָא (qara), "he read."

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]

Which English word descends from ق-ر-أ, and what does it mean in Arabic? (Quran — "the recitation.") Which letter carries the long ū of مَقْروء? (و.) Which earlier word shares the fused آ? (آكِل, ākil, "an eater.")

lessons.title: سأل (saʾala) — "he asked," and the Arabic word for answerable
lessons.gloss: "he asked" — one root that builds a question, a problem, an asker and the word for being answerable, plus the Hebrew twin hiding inside the name Saul

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: Hamza sat at the end of the last word. Here it sits in the middle — and as the vowels shift around it, it changes seats without changing sound at all.
Nothing new: س (sīn), أ (hamza on its alif seat) and ل (lām). Right to left, sa-ʾa-la.
What is worth doing is watching that seat move while the root holds still:
سَأَلَ (saʾala) — the a keeps hamza on ا.
سُؤال (suʾāl) — the u pulls it onto و.
سائِل (sāʾil) — the i pulls it onto dotless ي.
One consonant, one root, three spellings — exactly the rule laid out with qaraʾa, now doing its work inside a single family.
سَأَلَ (saʾala) = "he asked." Root س-أ-ل, the plain faʿala shape.
سُؤال (suʾāl) — "a question."
سائِل (sāʾil) — "an asker," the doer shape that also gave qāriʾ, "a reader."
مَسْأَلة (masʾala) — the ma- shape: "a matter, a problem" — a thing asked about.

مَسْؤول (masʾūl) — the done-to shape, literally "asked-of," and so "responsible"; as a noun, "an official." Arabic builds accountability out of being the one who gets questioned, which is a fair account of what accountability is.

The Hebrew twin is exact: שָׁאַל (shaʾal), "he asked" — Arabic s against Hebrew sh, the same swap heard between salām and shalom. Its passive participle is the name שָׁאוּל (Shaʾul), English Saul: "asked for." From the Arabic root, English took nothing.

segments.source: [PAUSE 1s]

What does the name Saul mean? ("Asked for" — from Hebrew shaʾal, twin of سَأَلَ.)

lessons.title: كتب (kataba) — "he wrote," and the root that furnishes a library
lessons.gloss: "he wrote" — the chapter's payoff, where one root and the patterns you already own hand you a book, a writer, an office and a library with nothing new to memorise

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.source: [PAUSE 2s]

segments.text: The chapter closes on the root every Arabic grammar reaches for first. Three letters — and you already own every pattern they need.

ك (kāf), ت (tāʾ, two dots) and ب (bāʾ, one dot below) were taught long ago. New is how they sit together: all three join, so كتب (kataba) is one unbroken run of pen — unlike ذهب, where dhāl refuses to connect, or أكل, where the alif stands off alone.
One old mark earns its keep too: put ة (tāʾ marbūṭa) on مَكْتَب (maktab) and you get مَكْتَبة (maktaba). One letter, and an office becomes a library.
كَتَبَ (kataba) = "he wrote." Root ك-ت-ب, plain faʿala shape. Now pour it through the patterns this track has handed you:
كِتاب (kitāb) — "a book." A written thing.
كاتِب (kātib) — "a writer," the doer shape of qāʾil and qāriʾ.
مَكْتوب (maktūb) — "written," the done-to shape of maqūl and mafhūm — and in speech, what has been written for you: fate.
مَكْتَب (maktab) — the ma- place shape of madhhab and masjid: the place of writing, a desk, an office.
مَكْتَبة (maktaba) — that place plus ة: a library.
Five words off one root, not one of them learned separately. That is the whole return on the root system, collected in one lesson.

No English word descends from ك-ت-ب. English does hold one from the same Semitic root, by way of Hebrew: a ketubah, the written Jewish marriage contract — כְּתוּבָּה (ketubbah), "a written thing," from כָּתַב (katav), "he wrote." That is maktūb's own pattern in the other language.

Which English word comes from this root? (None — but ketubah comes from its Hebrew twin katav.)
